outcome: No proof, disproof, counterexample, or record verification bound extension was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open with the same computational verification limit (7,110,200) reported before and after the frozen revision.
summary: The juggler sequence conjecture (does every positive integer's juggler sequence terminate at 1?) shows no change since 26 January 2024. The current Wikipedia article, MathWorld, HandWiki, Googology Wiki, and multiple search passes all report the same verification bound — all starting values up to 7,110,200 confirmed to reach 1 — that predates the frozen revision; this is not new progress, just the same longstanding figure being repeated. No preprint, announcement, or repository posting claiming a proof, disproof, explicit counterexample, or an extended/improved verification bound was found on arXiv, OEIS, or in general web search. OEIS A094679 (record-setting iteration counts) received a routine data contribution from Ethan Slota on 2025-04-15 adding one further record-holder term, but this is incremental computational tabulation of record-setters, not a movement of the existence question itself, and per §3.1 an existence/infinitude-style question is not advanced merely by extending a record table — it is not a bullet 'asking for a largest known object or the value of a constant.' A search for AI involvement in this problem turned up nothing genuine: the only AI-adjacent hit was an unrelated 2026 story about an AI-assisted counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, a completely different problem. I also found a claim on Grokipedia (an AI-generated encyclopedia) that 'Recent 2025 research has provided the first estimates of the maximum excursion constant and stopping constant for juggler-like sequences,' citing a reference labeled roughly 'Estimates of the maximum excursion constant and stopping constant...' on ResearchGate. I could not locate this paper through direct search on arXiv, ResearchGate title search, or Google — Grokipedia's own citation was truncated and did not resolve to a checkable author list, venue, or identifier. Because I could not verify this source exists or read its actual content, I am not treating it as an established event; a heuristic/stochastic estimate of excursion statistics (analogous to existing 3x+1 stochastic-model literature) would in any case likely be `progress` at best under these rules, not a resolution, and does not touch the existence question directly. I searched for a general arXiv paper on juggler sequences from 2024-2026 directly (via listing searches and targeted queries) and found none. Overall this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' case, consistent with the triage's 'none' verdict, which I confirm rather than dispute.
competing_reading: If the Grokipedia-cited 2025 paper on maximum-excursion/stopping constants for juggler-like sequences is real, it could constitute a `progress` event (a heuristic model producing new quantitative estimates), similar to long-standing stochastic-model work on the Collatz/3x+1 problem. I was unable to confirm its existence, authors, or content through direct search, so I have not recorded it as an event. Its absence from arXiv and ResearchGate direct search raises the possibility it is a Grokipedia hallucination — Grokipedia is machine-generated and known to sometimes fabricate or mis-cite sources.
what_would_settle_it: Locating the actual paper Grokipedia references (full author list, venue, arXiv ID or DOI) and reading its contribution statement would settle whether this is a genuine 2025 event and, if so, whether it involved any AI system and whether it counts as `progress` on the maximum-excursion/stopping-constant estimates (not on the core existence question).
